shape.name: Shape F - Productive Skills (Traditional)
shape.description: Traditional productive skills lesson with preparation stages followed by speaking or writing output.
shape.pedagogical_justification: Here the focus is on helping learners practice their speaking or writing skills. The lesson can usually be divided into preparation for speaking/writing and speaking/writing task stages.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to [speak/write] about [topic].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to plan a compare-and-contrast essay by analysing a model, generating ideas, and ordering their strongest points with linking expressions.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
05-08-26
Duration:
46 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1
Lesson Shape:
F (Productive Skills - Writing)
Materials:
Textbook writing workshop pp. 132-134, slideshow, essay question cards, planning worksheet
Assessment:
Written essay plan (notes and ordered sentences)
Skills:
Writing

stages.stage_aim: To reactivate lesson 1 and set the theme: today we study the model essay and plan our own
procedure: Show the splash slide. Ask: "What do you see? What might this lesson be about?" Let students guess.
Advance to the title slide: "Learn the shape. Plan your essay." Confirm the theme.
Show the "Why is this lesson important?" slide and read the bullets aloud.
Pairs recap lesson 1: "What are the four parts of a question? Which side did you choose?" Point to the Opinion-Reason-Evidence line on the slide.

stages.stage_aim: To analyse the four-paragraph structure of the model essay and answer Exercise 1
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "The model essay."
Display the structure map: introduction, paragraph 2, paragraph 3, conclusion. Point at each paragraph of the model on page 133.
Read the model essay together.

Work through Exercise 1 on page 132, one question at a time, revealing each answer on click: the number of paragraphs, the function of each paragraph, the writer's overall opinion, and the two meanings of "there is no 'I' in team".
Teach the comparing and contrasting strategy table: argue each side in turn, then conclude with your preference.

stages.stage_aim: For students to complete the notes comparing team and individual sports (Exercise 2)
procedure: Project the Exercise 2 answer slide.
Students complete the four notes about team and individual sports using the model essay.
Reveal the four answers row by row and check understanding of each gap.

stages.stage_aim: For pairs to generate positives and negatives for both aspects of their own topic (Exercise 4)
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Plan your essay."
Project the Exercise 4 task slide. In pairs, students think of positives and negatives for both aspects of their own essay topic.
Students write their ideas in the positives/negatives table on the worksheet.
Monitor and encourage ideas in both columns for both aspects.

stages.stage_aim: For students to choose their strongest ideas, learn the linking expressions, and write sentences to introduce them
procedure: Teach the selecting and ordering strategy: choose the strongest three or four ideas.
Reveal the Exercise 6 expression matches. Students compare them with the model essay.
Exercises 5 and 7: students choose their best ideas and write full sentences using the expressions.
Collect the plans at the end of the stage.

stages.stage_aim: To consolidate the plan and preview lesson 3: drafting
procedure: Show the wrap-up slide: "Your plan is ready."
Preview lesson 3: drafting the introduction, body, and conclusion from the plan.

shape.note: For middle schoolers interested in SCR approach to productive skills, see Shape J instead.

metadata.topic: Compare and contrast essays: the model essay and planning
materials: Textbook writing workshop — "A compare and contrast essay", pp. 132–134 (model essay, Exercises 1–7)
Slideshow — Lesson 2: The Model Essay and Planning
Essay question cards — each student's topic from Lesson 1
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to plan a compare-and-contrast essay by analysing a model essay, generating ideas, and ordering their strongest points with linking expressions.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: Learners will also be better able to identify the four-paragraph structure of an essay and the function of each paragraph.
answer_key: The model essay has four paragraphs: an introduction, two body paragraphs, and a conclusion.
The introduction asks the question. Paragraph 2 argues for individual sports. Paragraph 3 argues for team sports. The conclusion gives the writer's opinion.
The writer's overall opinion is that team sports are better for young people.
The idiom has two meanings. Literally, the word team has no letter i. Its real meaning is that the team matters more than any one player.
Exercise 2 — Notes on team and individual sports (p. 132)
Team sports have to be organized with others.
Learning to cooperate with others is more valuable.
Being part of a team can lead to arguments.
Let's start by looking at means the same as Let's begin with.
Then there's the fact that means the same as Another point is that.
In addition means the same as Also.
What's more means the same as Furthermore.
Finally means the same as Last but not least.
To conclude means the same as In conclusion.
